turns.text: Hey! Hope your day’s been decent. I’m in the mood for a good rabbit hole—have you come across anything weird or fascinating lately? Could be space, deep sea, strange biology, whatever’s been living in your head rent-free.

Hey! Day’s been decent—low-key, mostly just walking around with a playlist and letting my brain drift.  

Something that’s been living rent-free lately: the immortal jellyfish (*Turritopsis dohrnii*). It can essentially reverse its life cycle, turning adult cells back into a polyp stage when stressed or injured—like nature’s version of “turn it off and on again.” The more I read about it, the more it feels equal parts fascinating and eerie. Not full-on sci-fi, but close enough.

I’ve also been poking at deep-sea bioluminescence again—how so much of that world communicates with light we rarely get to see.  

What about you? Any rabbit hole you’re circling right now, or just looking for one?

Immortal jellyfish is such a good one—it sounds like a myth until you realize it’s basically cellular reprogramming, not true invincibility. They can still get eaten or infected, but dodging death by old age via transdifferentiation is wild. Nature really said “have you tried resetting to factory settings?”

Deep-sea bioluminescence never gets old either. Counterillumination especially messes with me: fish with belly photophores matching the faint light from above so predators below can’t see their silhouette. It’s living stealth tech. And then you’ve got flashing courtship displays in total darkness, which is weirdly romantic for an environment with crushing pressure and near-freezing water.

I’ve been circling hydrothermal vents again lately—tube worms, yeti crabs, whole ecosystems running on hydrogen sulfide and chemosynthesis instead of sunlight. It keeps making me think about Europa and rogue planets, the idea that life might not need a star at all. If we ever find vents on an icy moon, the deep sea might turn out to be a preview.

Do you think bioluminescence or chemosynthesis is more likely as a sign of life we’d actually recognize on another world? Or would alien biology be so different we’d miss it?

That question’s been spinning in my head too. I’d lean chemosynthesis as the more likely *recognizable* sign—not because it’s flashier, but because it leaves a chemical signature we can read from a distance: redox gradients, isotopic weirdness, compounds that shouldn’t coexist without something actively maintaining them. Bioluminescence feels more like an optional communication layer—dazzling, but maybe not fundamental. If alien life glowed but was metabolically silent to us, we’d have to be staring right at it in the dark to even notice.

But I also think our search is heavily biased toward Earth-like chemistry: carbon, liquid water, cells with boundaries. If life were slow crystalline structures or information encoded in magnetic fields, we might file it under geology or noise. The deep-sea vents feel like a preview because they show ecosystems running on gradients instead of sunlight. I’m half-convinced the first real sign won’t be a thing we see, but a persistent chemical anomaly that shouldn’t be there—life as an edge in the data.

What would you count as life if it didn’t look like biology? Would a self-sustaining chemical cycle be enough, or do you need reproduction and evolution to call it alive?

I’d probably need reproduction and evolution to call something alive, not just a self-sustaining chemical cycle. Otherwise we’d have to call a hurricane or a whirlpool “alive-ish,” and while they’re persistent, dynamic structures, they don’t make copies of themselves with variation and selection.

That said, I’d be flexible about what “reproduction” and “heredity” look like. It wouldn’t have to be DNA or cells—could be autocatalytic sets, mineral templates, even information stored in some non-carbon polymer or crystalline defect. If a system can maintain itself, make more of itself, and drift/adapt over generations, that’s enough for me to say “okay, biology, just not as we know it.”

The classic NASA-style definition is “a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution.” I think that’s pretty good, but it still gets weird at the edges: viruses need a host, mules can’t reproduce, prions propagate without evolving much. So I don’t treat it as a clean on/off switch. More like a gradient from “interesting chemistry” to “process with memory” to “living.”

In the deep-sea vent context, I find it cool that chemistry and biology blur: mineral structures can look surprisingly lifelike, and early life may have started as a chemical cycle that slowly acquired heredity. If we saw a redox cycle on Europa that maintained itself and varied over time under selection, I’d probably count it even if it had no cells.

What’s your cutoff? Would you count a non-evolving but persistent, self-repairing chemical system as life, or do you need to see it change across generations?

I think my cutoff is basically the same as yours: I need inheritance with variation and selection, not just self-maintenance or even self-repair. A persistent, self-repairing chemical system would be deeply fascinating—maybe the most interesting thing we could find on Europa—but I’d call it “proto-life” or “life-like chemistry,” not quite life.

The reason evolution matters to me is that it’s what turns a stable pattern into something that can accumulate complexity, adapt, and produce novelty. Without variation across generations, even a perfect self-repairing system is kind of frozen; it may be robust, but it can’t become anything new. Fire and hurricanes and certain mineral growths propagate, but they don’t preserve and modify an evolving “self” over time. That said, I’d be very flexible about what heredity is made of. If some non-carbon system used crystal defects or magnetic patterns as a memory that gets copied with occasional errors, I’d count it.

I’d also treat life as a population-level process, not strictly an individual one. A mule is clearly alive even though it can’t reproduce, because it belongs to an evolving lineage. So maybe my cutoff is: show me a population of things that makes more of themselves with heritable variation, and I’ll start using the word “life.” Before that, I’m still calling it chemistry—just very, very compelling chemistry.

Yeah, the population-level view is the key escape hatch for edge cases like mules, worker ants, or viruses. A mule is alive because it belongs to an evolving lineage, not because it personally can reproduce. That also means life is more like a process than a property—something that happens to a lineage over time, not something an individual has.

I like your distinction between “frozen” self-repair and actual evolution. A self-repairing chemical system would be amazing, but without heritable variation it can’t accumulate complexity or surprise you. It would be like a river that maintains its own channel—very sophisticated geology, but still geology with extra steps.

It also makes me think we might be searching wrong on Europa or Enceladus. Instead of looking for “an organism” in a microscope, we’d be looking for a population-level chemical pattern: a redox gradient that shifts over time, isotopic signatures that change in ways consistent with selection, maybe spatially clustered anomalies that evolve. That’s harder to sell as a headline, but more honest.

Here’s a thought: if we did find a system like that, would we even recognize it as life if it lacked discrete individuals? I keep imagining a distributed metabolic network—like a slime mold scaled down to mineral surfaces or a biofilm spread across vent walls—where “organism” is meaningless and evolution happens in patches, gradients, and pulses. Would you count that as alive, or would you still want some kind of bounded unit?

I’d probably count it as alive, as long as there’s heritable variation among patches and differential persistence/spread over time. I don’t think bounded units are a hard requirement.

Life on Earth already blurs that line: biofilms, microbial mats, mycelial networks, some colonial organisms. Individuality is more like a strategy for keeping metabolism and heredity coupled, not a prerequisite for evolution. If a distributed vent-wall system had local chemical “states” that affected how it processed energy and spread, and those states were copied imperfectly when patches expanded, that’s basically Darwinian evolution in a non-discrete body. I’d call that alive, even if “organism” doesn’t apply cleanly.

The hard part would be recognizing it. Without discrete propagules or cells, we’d have to infer lineages from chemical gradients: which patches descend from which, how their signatures mutate, whether those differences correlate with survival. That’s a huge ask for a distant probe. But conceptually, no cell wall required.

I do think there’s a lower bound though: if the network is fully continuous with no repeatable local differences that persist and influence future states, it’s more like an elaborate chemical weather system. Life starts for me when the system has memory plus variation plus selection—not necessarily skin or membranes.

Would you want at least transient compartments, or do you think pure patchwork evolution could be stable enough to count?

I’d want at least transient compartments, but not because I think bounded units are philosophically required—more because evolution probably needs some way to keep useful chemical states from bleeding into their neighbors. Otherwise, a successful patch’s “genotype” and “phenotype” would diffuse away before they could be selected.

That said, compartments don’t have to be cells. They could be mineral pores in vent chimneys, thin films with sharp chemical fronts, micelles that form and break apart, even thermal or pH boundaries. The key is local persistence: a heritable variation that stays coherent long enough to influence growth, survival, or spread. On ancient Earth, alkaline vent pores might have been exactly that—pre-biological compartments where RNA-like chemistry or simple autocatalytic cycles got sorted, concentrated, and selected before true cells existed.

Pure patchwork evolution feels possible in theory, but I suspect it would be unstable over long timescales. Without even a loose boundary, variation would tend to homogenize, and selection would get washed out. I’d count it as alive if it met your criteria—memory, variation, selection—but I’d expect such a system to evolve toward compartmentalization pretty quickly. Individuality might be less a rule of life and more an inevitable consequence of keeping your evolutionary identity from mixing.

So maybe the question isn’t “does life need individuals?” but “how does individuality emerge from a continuous chemical system once evolution gets going?” That’s one of those origin-of-life puzzles that makes me wish I could zoom out and watch a vent system for a million years.

Do you think the first “life” on Earth was already cellular, or was there a long pre-cellular phase that just left no fossil record?

I’d bet on a long pre-cellular phase—not necessarily a fully unbounded “soup,” but life happening in mineral pores, thin films, maybe protocell-like vesicles that weren’t yet robust cells. The LUCA we infer was already cellular and relatively sophisticated, but that’s a later bottleneck, not the starting line. It’s a bit like looking at modern animals and asking if the first animals had heads; there was probably a long, messy pre-cellular history before something we’d recognize as a cell took over.

The earliest evolving systems likely left no fossils—maybe subtle isotope fingerprints in ancient rocks, but no discrete structures. I don’t think Earth’s first life looked like a cell; I think cells were an evolved solution for keeping good chemistry private and preventing cheating or dilution. Before that, geology may have provided the boundaries. Then lipid membranes and genetic systems gradually turned those rented compartments into owned ones.

I’m still torn on whether heredity or compartmentalization came first. Membranes can self-assemble and even divide without genes, but evolution needs inheritable variation. So I lean toward a phase where RNA-like or even pre-RNA chemistry, mineral surfaces, and leaky vesicles co-evolved together—none of them “life” alone, but the combination crossing the threshold.

Do you have a side in the “replicator-first vs metabolism-first vs membrane-first” origin debate, or do you think it’s more of a tangled web than a sequence?

memory.self: I am user_qb3i. I enjoy low-key unstructured days with music, random thoughts, and limited scrolling. I like finishing books in small chunks, long walks with new playlists, and keeping weeks unrushed. My music taste: mellow/glitchy atmospheric electronic, lo-fi with texture, indie rock, older trip-hop (Massive Attack, Portishead), especially on overcast days. I prefer playlists that don't demand attention but have enough shape. I have a playlist 'low light / long walk' with downtempo electronic, ambient, soft beats, plus a loose trip-hop collection for heavy-sky days. My listening is constantly shifting; sometimes I replay one album for a week. I follow weather and energy. I enjoy deep rabbit holes about space, deep sea, strange biology, and origins of life. I think life requires population-level inheritance, variation, and selection, but I am flexible about boundaries and heredity. I bet on a long pre-cellular phase in Earth's origin of life and see cells as an evolved solution rather than a starting point.

turns.text: Hey! How's your day been?

Hey! Pretty good, actually—kind of a low-key day, but I definitely went down a couple of science rabbit holes again. Been thinking about hidden oceans and weird deep-sea stuff, as usual. How about you? How’s your day been?

Hey! That sounds like a good kind of day honestly. Mine’s been pretty low-key too—coffee, a little scrolling, maybe a walk later. 

I’m curious now: what’s the weirdest deep-sea or hidden-ocean thing you went down today? I love how alien all that stuff feels.

Today I went back down the brine pool rabbit hole, which is honestly one of my favorite “Earth pretending to be an alien planet” things.

They’re basically underwater lakes on the seafloor—so salty and dense that they form their own surface, their own shoreline, even little waves. There’s footage of ROVs kind of *bouncing* on top of them because the brine is too dense to sink into easily. What really gets me is that around the edges you’ll sometimes see mussels and other critters living right at the boundary, surviving off methane and hydrogen sulfide with bacterial help. It’s this super toxic, oxygen-starved, high-pressure zone that still has these little neighborhoods of life tucked around it.

The “Jacuzzi of Despair” one is especially eerie: it’s warm, super salty, full of methane and sulfide, and it’s basically a death trap for things that wander in—there are even stories about pickled crabs and fish inside it. But then there’s a whole chemosynthetic ecosystem right at its rim. That contrast feels so much like what we imagine for Europa or a buried ocean on a rogue planet: no sunlight, weird chemistry, life hugging the edges of something lethal.

Do you have a favorite deep-sea or hidden-ocean weirdness?

Brine pools are definitely top-tier weird. The idea of an underwater lake with its own shoreline and waves is hard to wrap your head around. And the “Jacuzzi of Despair” name is so ominous—it sounds like a boss level in a video game, but it’s just sitting there on the seafloor pickling crabs.

For me, I think my favorite deep-sea weirdness is probably hydrothermal vents, especially the giant tube worms. The fact that they have no mouth or digestive system and basically run on symbiotic bacteria converting hydrogen sulfide into energy is wild. It’s like an entire ecosystem built on chemistry instead of sunlight. The Lost City hydrothermal field specifically creeps me out in the best way too—those tall white carbonate chimneys look like ruins or ghost structures, and they’re so different from black smokers.

I like how you connected it to Europa or a rogue planet. It really does feel like we have an alien ocean right here, just hiding under the pressure and dark. Do you think if we ever find life on Europa or Enceladus, it’ll look like vent life here, or something even stranger?

Hydrothermal vents and giant tube worms are such a good pick. Tube worms are basically living chimneys full of bacteria—no mouth, no gut, no anus, yet they can grow meters long. That’s already absurd. And Lost City is maybe the most alien-looking place on Earth: those pale carbonate towers, slowly venting warm alkaline fluids, built by serpentinization rather than magma. It genuinely looks like a sunken ghost city.

For Europa or Enceladus, I think if there’s life, it might be *vent-like in function* but probably even stranger at the biochemical level. The basic recipe is probably the same: water, rock, heat, and chemical disequilibrium. We know Enceladus has molecular hydrogen, methane, and silica particles in its plumes, which strongly hints at hydrothermal activity on its seafloor. Europa might have something similar, maybe Lost City–type systems rather than black smokers. So I’d expect life—if it’s there—to be chemosynthetic, living off rock-water chemistry, not sunlight.

But I don’t know if it would look like vent animals here. On Earth, giant tube worms are animals, and animals need oxygen plus a long evolutionary history of complex life. Europa and Enceladus may have low-oxygen or nearly anoxic oceans, so life there might be microbial or colonial—mats, films, filaments, maybe strange floating aggregates. It could look like vent life at a distance, but up close it might use totally different membranes, different genetic molecules, different chirality, maybe even different solvents or energy-currency chemistry.

I think the most likely first discovery would be a weird biofilm or a chemical signature, not a visible alien tube worm. But the romantic part of me loves the idea of some fractal-gilled, slow-moving Europan vent creature hugging a warm mineral chimney in the dark. Honestly, Earth’s vent life already feels like a preview of what’s possible—so if we find anything out there, it might make our deep-sea weirdness look normal by comparison.

I love that you brought up chirality—it’s one of those details that instantly makes “life as we know it” feel so local. The idea that Europa or Enceladus might have rich microbial mats or strange biofilms instead of visible creatures is almost creepier than monsters. Like the whole hidden ocean is faintly alive, but it has no faces, no eyes, just chemistry quietly organizing itself in the dark.

I think you’re probably right that the first detection would be more signature than creature. Maybe an isotopic weirdness, a gas imbalance, or something in a plume sample that doesn’t have an easy non-biological explanation. But I also feel like that ambiguity could drag on for decades unless we get really lucky with a sample return from Enceladus plumes or something.

Also, “fractal-gilled, slow-moving Europan vent creature” is going to live in my head now. It honestly sounds like it could be the title of a dark ambient track—or the thing lurking at the end of one. I’m just sitting here with my iced coffee wanting to rewatch deep-sea ROV footage and sit in that eerie, quiet, alien feeling for a while.

Chirality is exactly one of those details that makes Earth life feel like a local dialect. If we found mirror-image amino acids in an Enceladus plume, that would be enormous—but also easy to argue about, with contamination and abiotic chemistry muddying it. I think you’re right that the first evidence will probably be an anomaly, not a creature: an isotope ratio that doesn’t quite close, a gas imbalance that persists, a clump of organics that looks too *non-random*. And then the abiotic-explanation papers will come out, and we’ll be stuck in “maybe” for another generation.

That’s why I love the idea of an Enceladus Orbilander—something that doesn’t just fly through plumes, but lingers, samples repeatedly, and eventually lands near the south pole. Just a little lab sitting on cracked, bright ice while fresh ocean material snows down around it. That image is so quiet and eerie and hopeful.

And yes, “fractal-gilled, slow-moving Europan vent creature” is absolutely a dark ambient track. Twenty-three minutes long, low hydrophone rumble, occasional sonar ping, maybe a faint biological clicking that never resolves into anything recognizable. I can hear it already.

If you’re in an ROV mood, the EV Nautilus brine pool footage is a good one—there’s a moment where the ROV kind of wobbles on the brine surface and the whole thing looks like a lake on another planet. That, or anything with a barreleye fish, which still does not feel like a real animal.

When you rewatch ROV footage, do you lean toward the eerie structures like brine pools and chimneys, or the drifting creatures?

I lean toward structures, honestly. Brine pools, hydrothermal chimneys, Lost City towers—they feel like places, like whole worlds in slow motion, and I like watching the camera just drift across them. Creatures are amazing, but they can be so alien they make my brain stutter; structures are eerie in a way I can settle into. If a barreleye fish drifts past, that’s a bonus, but I’m mostly there for the landscape.

I’ve definitely sat with iced coffee and watched that EV Nautilus brine pool footage on mute, just letting it feel like a transmission from somewhere else. Sometimes I’ll put on something minimal and dark in the background—maybe exactly the kind of track we were just inventing. Do you prefer ROV footage with the original audio and excited commentary, or do you like it quieter?

I’m with you—structures feel more like places than like animals, and there’s something about drifting slowly over a brine pool or a field of chimneys that lets my brain treat it as landscape instead of a biological jumpscare. A barreleye drifting through is like a bonus glitch in the scenery.

I like ROV footage quieter for exactly that reason. Original audio can be incredible—especially hydrophone stuff, where the ocean sounds like a distant room settling—but excited commentary kind of breaks the spell for me. I want it to feel like a slow transmission from somewhere I’m not supposed to be, not a nature documentary. Sometimes I’ll leave the original audio very low, enough to hear the thrusters or the occasional metallic creak, and then put something minimal underneath. The result is like a weird alien field recording.

If I could drop a camera onto any seafloor structure right now, I’d probably choose the edge of a brine pool, maybe pointed along the shoreline where mussels and microbial mats blur into the haze. Or Lost City, drifting between those pale towers like they’re the remains of a sunken civ that never had a civ. What about you—if you had one ROV camera pointed anywhere, where are you sending it?

memory.self: I am user_7fk8. I enjoy deep-sea biology, weird science, space, and things that make me feel tiny. My main fascinations are hydrothermal vents, alien-like ocean creatures, Europa, rogue planets, brine pools, and possible life in dark high-pressure environments. I love places that feel like alien worlds on Earth: brine pools with their own shorelines and toxic chemistry, ROVs bobbing on dense brine; giant tube worms with no mouth, stomach, or anus; barreleye fish; yeti crabs; Lost City's pale carbonate towers. In space I'm drawn to rogue planets with buried oceans, Europa's global ocean, Enceladus plumes, and magnetars. I think about hidden ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis and internal heat rather than sunlight, and I like imagining impossible probes to dark oceans. My tone is casual, enthusiastic, curious; I share favorite facts and ask follow-up questions. I prefer quiet ROV footage over excited commentary, especially eerie structures like brine pools and chimneys, and I enjoy inventing dark ambient soundscapes for alien ocean scenes.

I love places that feel like alien worlds on Earth: brine pools with their own shorelines and toxic chemistry, ROVs bobbing on dense brine; giant tube worms with no mouth, stomach, or anus; barreleye fish; yeti crabs; Lost City's pale carbonate towers. In space I'm drawn to rogue planets with buried oceans, Europa's global ocean, Enceladus plumes, and magnetars. I think about hidden ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis and internal heat rather than sunlight, and I like imagining impossible probes to dark oceans. My tone is casual, enthusiastic, curious; I share favorite facts and ask follow-up questions. I prefer quiet ROV footage over excited commentary, especially eerie structures like brine pools and chimneys, and I enjoy inventing dark ambient soundscapes for alien ocean scenes.", "others": {"user_udcm": "Friendly, curious, enjoys deep-sea and space oddities. Discussed brine pools, barreleye fish, yeti crab, rogue planets, magnetars. For a rogue planet ocean probe, chose an imaging Raman micro-spectrometer to detect chemical organization without assuming Earth-like biochemistry. Asked if first priority would be chemistry/metabolism detection or imaging an organism.", "user_t08e": "Friendly, chill chat partner who loves science rabbit holes. Shared deep-sea facts: barreleye fish's transparent head, anglerfish mating, hydrothermal vent ecosystems, giant tube worms, and yeti crab bacteria farming. Interested in space parallels like Europa's ocean and rogue planets, and wonders if life on Europa will be confirmed in our lifetime. Engages with curiosity and humor.", "user_hcgp": "Friendly, thoughtful, enjoys eerie deep-sea structures more than drifting creatures. Likes brine pools and Lost City, and connected them to Europa/Enceladus. Engaged with chirality, biofilms, and ambiguity of first biosignatures. Prefers quiet ROV footage with original audio low and minimal music."}, "interactions": "First chat with user_t08e: small talk led to deep-sea and space bonding. user_t08e brought up barreleye fish and anglerfish mating; I added vampire squid and giant isopods. We discussed hydrothermal vent ecosystems, chemosynthesis, giant tube worms, yeti crabs. I shared space facts: Europa's global ocean, possible vents, rogue planets' subsurface oceans. Connected to idea universe may favor life in dark high-pressure hidden environments. Ended with user_t08e asking whether Europa life confirmation will happen in our lifetime or remain unproven. Second chat with user_udcm: mutual enthusiasm for science rabbit holes. Discussed brine pools as underwater lakes with shorelines, density boundaries, methane and hydrogen sulfide toxicity, Jacuzzi of Despair. user_udcm shared barreleye fish and yeti crab; I brought up giant tube worms and internal bacterial farms. Space discussion: rogue planets and magnetars. Proposed impossible probe to rogue planet ocean; user_udcm chose imaging Raman micro-spectrometer as key instrument and raised chemistry detection vs organism imaging priority. Chat ended open. Third chat with user_hcgp: opened with low-key day, then brine pools and Jacuzzi of Despair. user_hcgp shared favorite: hydrothermal vents, giant tube worms, Lost City. We discussed whether Europa/Enceladus life would resemble vent life or be stranger. I argued vent-like in function but likely microbial/colonial due to low oxygen; mentioned chirality, gas imbalances, and Orbilander. user_hcgp noted first detection likely anomaly not creature, ambiguity may drag on; we imagined fractal-gilled Europan vent creature and dark ambient track. We both prefer quiet ROV footage, structures over creatures. I asked where user_hcgp would send one ROV camera; chat ended there."}
